# Radix Sort Benchmark Results — Maleoon 935

Date: 2026-06-10

## Test Environment

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| **Device** | HarmonyOS arm64 phone |
| **GPU** | Maleoon 935, Vulkan 1.4.309, subgroupSize=32 |
| **CPU** | Kirin big.LITTLE: 4×1.72 GHz + 8×2.27 GHz + 2×2.75 GHz |
| **CPU sort** | `std::sort` / `std::stable_sort`, pinned to big cores (cpu12-13, 2.75 GHz) |
| **Frequency** | All 14 CPU cores locked to max via `scaling_min_freq = scaling_max_freq` |
| **GPU timing** | `vkCmdWriteTimestamp` (ALL_COMMANDS_BIT) × `timestampPeriod` (~107 ns/tick), envelope |
| **CPU timing** | `std::chrono::high_resolution_clock` for `std::sort` |
| **Build** | HarmonyOS NDK cross-compiled, `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` |
| **Sizes** | 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K, 32K, 64K, 128K, 256K, 512K, 1M |

## Algorithms Compared

| Algorithm | Source | Dispatch/Pass | Pipeline | Warmup | Runs |
|-----------|--------|---------------|----------|--------|------|
| **CPU std::sort** | C++ STL | — | — | 5 | 10 (median) |
| **vulkan_radix_sort** | [vulkan_radix_sort](.) | 3 dispatch/pass (upsweep→spine→downsweep) × 4 passes | Created once | 5 | 10 (median) |
| **VkRadixSort Multi** | [VkRadixSort](../VkRadixSort) | 2 dispatch/pass (histogram→scatter) × 4 passes | Created once (reused) | 5 | 10 (median) |

Both GPU radix sorts operate on 32-bit unsigned integers (full range `[0, 2³²-1]`) with 4 × 8-bit radix passes and `WORKGROUP_SIZE=256`.

## Timing Methodology

Both GPU implementations use `vkCmdWriteTimestamp` with `VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_ALL_COMMANDS_BIT` to measure the **envelope** time from first to last timestamp:

- **vulkan_radix_sort**: 2 timestamps (start/end) around the entire sort command buffer → single envelope
- **VkRadixSort Multi**: 8 timestamps (2 per iteration × 4 iterations) → envelope from first to last timestamp

This captures the full GPU pipeline including barriers, fill buffer, and inter-dispatch synchronization, making the measurements directly comparable.

## Full Comparison (Locked Max Freq, Fair Settings)

![Three-way comparison](benchmark_comparison_full.png)

### Keys-only Sort (GPU timestamp envelope, median of 10 runs)

| N | CPU (ms) | vulkan_radix_sort (ms) | VkRadixSort Multi (ms) | vrs/CPU | vkr/CPU | vkr/vrs |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1K | 0.038 | 0.686 | 0.729 | 0.06× | 0.05× | 1.06× |
| 2K | 0.078 | 0.825 | 0.816 | 0.09× | 0.10× | **0.99×** |
| 4K | 0.166 | 0.857 | 1.000 | 0.19× | 0.17× | 1.17× |
| 8K | 0.351 | 0.893 | 1.485 | 0.39× | 0.24× | 1.66× |
| 16K | 0.764 | 0.939 | 1.521 | 0.81× | 0.50× | 1.62× |
| **32K** | **1.653** | **1.197** | **2.265** | **1.38×** | 0.73× | 1.89× |
| 64K | 3.562 | 1.967 | 3.336 | 1.81× | **1.07×** | 1.70× |
| 128K | 7.537 | 3.471 | 5.039 | 2.17× | 1.50× | 1.45× |
| 256K | 15.955 | 5.305 | 9.350 | 3.01× | 1.71× | 1.76× |
| 512K | 34.154 | 8.625 | 16.091 | 3.96× | 2.12× | 1.87× |
| **1M** | **71.478** | **16.089** | **20.204** | **4.44×** | **3.54×** | **1.26×** |

> **vrs/CPU** = CPU time / vulkan_radix_sort time (>1 = GPU faster)
> **vkr/CPU** = CPU time / VkRadixSort time (>1 = GPU faster)
> **vkr/vrs** = VkRadixSort time / vulkan_radix_sort time (>1 = vulkan_radix_sort faster, <1 = VkRadixSort faster)

### Key-Value Sort (vulkan_radix_sort only)

| N | CPU kv (ms) | vrs kv GPU (ms) | GPU Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1K | 0.054 | 0.887 | 0.06× |
| 2K | 0.116 | 0.931 | 0.12× |
| 4K | 0.220 | 0.963 | 0.23× |
| 8K | 0.512 | 1.017 | 0.50× |
| 16K | 1.014 | 1.133 | 0.89× |
| **32K** | **2.375** | **1.630** | **1.46×** |
| 64K | 4.773 | 2.763 | 1.73× |
| 128K | 11.005 | 3.665 | 3.00× |
| 256K | 22.136 | 6.293 | 3.52× |
| 512K | 50.647 | 10.909 | 4.64× |
| **1M** | **105.362** | **18.532** | **5.69×** |

### Scaling Curves

![Scaling comparison](benchmark_comparison_scaling.png)

## Key Findings

### 1. Crossover Points

| Algorithm | Crossover N | Speedup at Crossover |
|-----------|:-----------:|:--------------------:|
| vulkan_radix_sort | **32K** | 1.38× |
| VkRadixSort Multi | **64K** | 1.07× |

At N < 32K, CPU `std::sort` is faster due to GPU launch overhead (~0.7 ms latency floor).

### 2. vulkan_radix_sort vs VkRadixSort Multi

| Size Range | vkr/vrs | Winner | Margin |
|------------|:-------:|--------|--------|
| 2K | 0.99× | **Tied** | — |
| 1K | 1.06× | Roughly equal | 6% |
| 4K | 1.17× | vulkan_radix_sort | 17% |
| 8K–16K | 1.62–1.66× | vulkan_radix_sort | 62–66% |
| 32K | 1.89× | vulkan_radix_sort | 89% |
| 64K–512K | 1.45–1.87× | vulkan_radix_sort | 45–87% |
| **1M** | **1.26×** | vulkan_radix_sort | 26% |

**At N=2K the two implementations are essentially tied (0.99×).** vulkan_radix_sort wins decisively at N ≥ 8K due to higher GPU utilization from its 3-pass architecture, with the gap peaking at N=32K (1.89×) and narrowing at N=1M (1.26×) as both saturate the GPU.

### 3. Peak Performance (N=1M, Locked)

| Sort | GPU (ms) | CPU (ms) | GPU Speedup |
|------|--------:|--------:|------------:|
| **vulkan_radix_sort keys** | 16.09 | 71.48 | **4.44×** |
| **vulkan_radix_sort kv** | 18.53 | 105.36 | **5.69×** |
| VkRadixSort Multi keys | 20.20 | 71.48 | 3.54× |

### 4. CPU Scaling

CPU `std::sort` at locked 2.75 GHz follows O(N log N) exactly. The normalized time T/(N·log₂N) converges to **~3.4 ns** for N ≥ 16K, which is ~9.4 clock cycles per comparison-swap on the Cortex core.

## Fair Comparison Methodology

All measurements use identical methodology:

1. **Same warmup**: 5 warmup runs before timing (both implementations)
2. **Same repeat count**: Median of 10 timed runs (both implementations)
3. **Same data range**: Full 32-bit `[0, 2³²-1]` uniform random integers (both implementations)
4. **Same timestamp stage**: `VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_ALL_COMMANDS_BIT` for all timestamps
5. **Same measurement type**: GPU timestamp envelope (first→last timestamp), not per-pass sum
6. **Same pipeline policy**: Vulkan pipeline created once, reused across all sizes
7. **Same frequency**: All 14 CPU cores locked to max frequency
8. **Correctness verified**: Each run verified against CPU `std::sort` result

### Remaining inherent differences

| Aspect | vulkan_radix_sort | VkRadixSort Multi |
|--------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Submit pattern | Single command buffer per sort | 4 command buffers, semaphore-chained |
| Dispatch count | 12 (3 × 4 passes) | 8 (2 × 4 passes) |
| Pipeline barriers | Between upsweep/spine/downsweep | Between histogram/scatter |
| Timestamp count | 2 (single envelope) | 8 (envelope from first to last) |

These are inherent to each algorithm's design and represent real-world performance characteristics.

## Device Info

- **SoC**: Kirin (ARM big.LITTLE, 14 cores)
- **CPU topology**: 4×1.72 GHz (LITTLE) + 8×2.27 GHz (mid) + 2×2.75 GHz (big)
- **GPU**: Maleoon 935, Vulkan 1.4.309
- **subgroupSize**: 32, maxComputeInvocations=1024, maxSharedMemory=32768
- **timestampPeriod**: ~107 ns/tick

## Raw Data

- `vulkan_perf_locked.csv` — vulkan_radix_sort GPU, locked max freq
- `cpu_perf_locked.csv` — CPU std::sort, locked max freq
- `benchmark_comparison_full.png` — 3-panel comparison chart
- `benchmark_comparison_scaling.png` — log-log scaling curves

# Verification Before Completion

## Overview

Claiming work is complete without verification is dishonesty, not efficiency.

**Core principle:** Evidence before claims, always.

**Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
```

If you haven't run the verification command in this message, you cannot claim it passes.

## The Gate Function

```
BEFORE claiming any status or expressing satisfaction:

1. IDENTIFY: What command proves this claim?
2. RUN: Execute the FULL command (fresh, complete)
3. READ: Full output, check exit code, count failures
4. VERIFY: Does output confirm the claim?
   - If NO: State actual status with evidence
   - If YES: State claim WITH evidence
5. ONLY THEN: Make the claim

Skip any step = lying, not verifying
```

## Common Failures

| Claim | Requires | Not Sufficient |
|-------|----------|----------------|
| Tests pass | Test command output: 0 failures | Previous run, "should pass" |
| Linter clean | Linter output: 0 errors | Partial check, extrapolation |
| Build succeeds | Build command: exit 0 | Linter passing, logs look good |
| Bug fixed | Test original symptom: passes | Code changed, assumed fixed |
| Regression test works | Red-green cycle verified | Test passes once |
| Agent completed | VCS diff shows changes | Agent reports "success" |
| Requirements met | Line-by-line checklist | Tests passing |

## Red Flags - STOP

- Using "should", "probably", "seems to"
- Expressing satisfaction before verification ("Great!", "Perfect!", "Done!", etc.)
- About to commit/push/PR without verification
- Trusting agent success reports
- Relying on partial verification
- Thinking "just this once"
- Tired and wanting work over
- **ANY wording implying success without having run verification**

## Rationalization Prevention

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Should work now" | RUN the verification |
| "I'm confident" | Confidence ≠ evidence |
| "Just this once" | No exceptions |
| "Linter passed" | Linter ≠ compiler |
| "Agent said success" | Verify independently |
| "I'm tired" | Exhaustion ≠ excuse |
| "Partial check is enough" | Partial proves nothing |
| "Different words so rule doesn't apply" | Spirit over letter |

## Key Patterns

**Tests:**
```
✅ [Run test command] [See: 34/34 pass] "All tests pass"
❌ "Should pass now" / "Looks correct"
```

**Regression tests (TDD Red-Green):**
```
✅ Write → Run (pass) → Revert fix → Run (MUST FAIL) → Restore → Run (pass)
❌ "I've written a regression test" (without red-green verification)
```

**Build:**
```
✅ [Run build] [See: exit 0] "Build passes"
❌ "Linter passed" (linter doesn't check compilation)
```

**Requirements:**
```
✅ Re-read plan → Create checklist → Verify each → Report gaps or completion
❌ "Tests pass, phase complete"
```

**Agent delegation:**
```
✅ Agent reports success → Check VCS diff → Verify changes → Report actual state
❌ Trust agent report
```

## Why This Matters

From 24 failure memories:
- your human partner said "I don't believe you" - trust broken
- Undefined functions shipped - would crash
- Missing requirements shipped - incomplete features
- Time wasted on false completion → redirect → rework
- Violates: "Honesty is a core value. If you lie, you'll be replaced."

## When To Apply

**ALWAYS before:**
- ANY variation of success/completion claims
- ANY expression of satisfaction
- ANY positive statement about work state
- Committing, PR creation, task completion
- Moving to next task
- Delegating to agents

**Rule applies to:**
- Exact phrases
- Paraphrases and synonyms
- Implications of success
- ANY communication suggesting completion/correctness

## The Bottom Line

**No shortcuts for verification.**

Run the command. Read the output. THEN claim the result.

This is non-negotiable.

Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-1000/bundled-skills/2.1.170/b69b889619cd6d950ae366837657155a/run

**Running means launching the actual app and interacting with it** —
not the test suite, not an `import` of an internal function and a
`console.log`. The app as a user (human or programmatic) would meet
it: the CLI at its command, the server at its socket, the GUI at its
window.

## First: does a project skill already cover this?

A project skill that launches this app is the repo's verified path —
its author already cold-started from a Linux container and committed
what worked: the exact `apt-get` line, the env vars, the patches, the
driver. Use it instead of rediscovering.

```bash
d=$PWD; while :; do
  grep -Hm1 '^description:' "$d"/.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md 2>/dev/null
  [ -e "$d/.git" ] || [ "$d" = / ] && break
  d=$(dirname "$d")
done
```

- **One describes launching/driving this app** → read that SKILL.md
  and follow it verbatim. Don't paraphrase; don't skip the patches.
- **Mega-repo, several plausible, no clear match** → ask the user
  which unit to run.
- **Stale** (fails on mechanics unrelated to your task) → tell the
  user; offer to refresh it via `/run-skill-generator`.
- **Nothing about running** → fall back to the patterns below.

## Otherwise: match the shape, use the pattern

Pick the row closest to your project. Each example walks through
launch + first interaction; ignore any trailing "write the skill"
section — you're using the recipe, not authoring one.

| Project type | Handle | Example |
|---|---|---|
| CLI tool | direct invocation, exit code, stdin/stdout | [examples/cli.md](examples/cli.md) |
| Web server / API | background launch + `curl` smoke | [examples/server.md](examples/server.md) |
| TUI / interactive terminal | tmux `send-keys` / `capture-pane` | [examples/tui.md](examples/tui.md) |
| Electron / desktop GUI | Playwright `_electron` REPL under xvfb | [examples/electron.md](examples/electron.md) |
| Browser-driven | dev server + `chromium-cli` script | [examples/playwright.md](examples/playwright.md) |
| Library / SDK | import-and-call smoke script at the package boundary | [examples/library.md](examples/library.md) |

If nothing fits, start from the closest match and adapt. For a web
app, [examples/playwright.md](examples/playwright.md) — drive it with
`chromium-cli`, no custom driver needed. For a desktop app,
[examples/electron.md](examples/electron.md) — it has the `_electron`
REPL driver skeleton and the tmux wrapping.

## Drive it, don't just launch it

Launching with no interaction proves the entrypoint resolves. That's
not running the app — it's typechecking with extra steps. Drive it to
a point where a user would see something:

- CLI → type a representative command, check the exit code and output.
- Server → hit the route the diff touches with `curl`, read the body.
- TUI → `send-keys` a navigation, `capture-pane` the result.
- GUI → click the button, screenshot the window. **Look at the
  screenshot.** A blank frame is a failure to launch.

If the fallback pattern didn't work out of the box — you had to
install packages, set env vars, patch config, or write a driver —
recommend `/run-skill-generator` in your report so that work gets
captured as a project skill. If it just worked, don't.

Both GPU radix sorts operate on 32-bit unsigned integers (full range `[0, 2³²-1]`) with 4 × 8-bit radix passes and `WORKGROUP_SIZE=256`.

## Timing Methodology

Both GPU implementations use `vkCmdWriteTimestamp` with `VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_ALL_COMMANDS_BIT` to measure the **envelope** time from first to last timestamp:

- **vulkan_radix_sort**: 2 timestamps (start/end) around the entire sort command buffer → single envelope

| **32K** | **1.653** | **1.197** | **2.265** | **1.38×** | 0.73× | 1.89× |

| 128K | 7.537 | 3.471 | 5.039 | 2.17× | 1.50× | 1.45× |
| 256K | 15.955 | 5.305 | 9.350 | 3.01× | 1.71× | 1.76× |
| 512K | 34.154 | 8.625 | 16.091 | 3.96× | 2.12× | 1.87× |
| **1M** | **71.478** | **16.089** | **20.204** | **4.44×** | **3.54×** | **1.26×** |

> **vrs/CPU** = CPU time / vulkan_radix_sort time (>1 = GPU faster)
> **vkr/CPU** = CPU time / VkRadixSort time (>1 = GPU faster)
> **vkr/vrs** = VkRadixSort time / vulkan_radix_sort time (>1 = vulkan_radix_sort faster, <1 = VkRadixSort faster)

| 64K | 4.773 | 2.763 | 1.73× |
| 128K | 11.005 | 3.665 | 3.00× |
| 256K | 22.136 | 6.293 | 3.52× |
| 512K | 50.647 | 10.909 | 4.64× |
| **1M** | **105.362** | **18.532** | **5.69×** |

### Scaling Curves

![Scaling comparison](benchmark_comparison_scaling.png)

## Key Findings

### 1. Crossover Points

| Algorithm | Crossover N | Speedup at Crossover |
|-----------|:-----------:|:--------------------:|
| vulkan_radix_sort | **32K** | 1.38× |
| VkRadixSort Multi | **64K** | 1.07× |

At N < 32K, CPU `std::sort` is faster due to GPU launch overhead (~0.7 ms latency floor).

### 2. vulkan_radix_sort vs VkRadixSort Multi

| Size Range | vkr/vrs | Winner | Margin |
|------------|:-------:|--------|--------|
| 2K | 0.99× | **Tied** | — |
| 1K | 1.06× | Roughly equal | 6% |
| 4K | 1.17× | vulkan_radix_sort | 17% |

| 32K | 1.89× | vulkan_radix_sort | 89% |

| **1M** | **1.26×** | vulkan_radix_sort | 26% |

**At N=2K the two implementations are essentially tied (0.99×).** vulkan_radix_sort wins decisively at N ≥ 8K due to higher GPU utilization from its 3-pass architecture, with the gap peaking at N=32K (1.89×) and narrowing at N=1M (1.26×) as both saturate the GPU.

| Pipeline barriers | Between upsweep/spine/downsweep | Between histogram/scatter |
| Timestamp count | 2 (single envelope) | 8 (envelope from first to last) |

| **vulkan_radix_sort** | [vulkan_radix_sort](.) | 3 dispatch/pass (upsweep→spine→downsweep) × 4 passes | Created once | 5 | 10 (median) |
| **VkRadixSort Multi** | [VkRadixSort](../VkRadixSort) | 2 dispatch/pass (histogram→scatter) × 4 passes | Created once (reused) | 5 | 10 (median) |

Both GPU radix sorts operate on 32-bit unsigned integers (full range `[0, 2³²-1]`) with 4 × 8-bit radix passes and `WORKGROUP_SIZE=256`.

## Timing Methodology

Both GPU implementations use `vkCmdWriteTimestamp` with `VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_ALL_COMMANDS_BIT` to measure the **envelope** time from first to last timestamp:

- **vulkan_radix_sort**: 2 timestamps (start/end) around the entire sort command buffer → single envelope
- **VkRadixSort Multi**: 8 timestamps (2 per iteration × 4 iterations) → envelope from first to last timestamp

This captures the full GPU pipeline including barriers, fill buffer, and inter-dispatch synchronization, making the measurements directly comparable.

![Scaling comparison](benchmark_comparison_scaling.png)

## Key Findings

### 1. Crossover Points

| Algorithm | Crossover N | Speedup at Crossover |
|-----------|:-----------:|:--------------------:|
| vulkan_radix_sort | **32K** | 1.38× |
| VkRadixSort Multi | **64K** | 1.07× |

At N < 32K, CPU `std::sort` is faster due to GPU launch overhead (~0.7 ms latency floor).

### 2. vulkan_radix_sort vs VkRadixSort Multi

| Size Range | vkr/vrs | Winner | Margin |
|------------|:-------:|--------|--------|
| 2K | 0.99× | **Tied** | — |
| 1K | 1.06× | Roughly equal | 6% |
| 4K | 1.17× | vulkan_radix_sort | 17% |
| 8K–16K | 1.62–1.66× | vulkan_radix_sort | 62–66% |
| 32K | 1.89× | vulkan_radix_sort | 89% |
| 64K–512K | 1.45–1.87× | vulkan_radix_sort | 45–87% |
| **1M** | **1.26×** | vulkan_radix_sort | 26% |

**At N=2K the two implementations are essentially tied (0.99×).** vulkan_radix_sort wins decisively at N ≥ 8K due to higher GPU utilization from its 3-pass architecture, with the gap peaking at N=32K (1.89×) and narrowing at N=1M (1.26×) as both saturate the GPU.

### 3. Peak Performance (N=1M, Locked)

| Sort | GPU (ms) | CPU (ms) | GPU Speedup |
|------|--------:|--------:|------------:|
| **vulkan_radix_sort keys** | 16.09 | 71.48 | **4.44×** |
| **vulkan_radix_sort kv** | 18.53 | 105.36 | **5.69×** |
| VkRadixSort Multi keys | 20.20 | 71.48 | 3.54× |

### 4. CPU Scaling

CPU `std::sort` at locked 2.75 GHz follows O(N log N) exactly. The normalized time T/(N·log₂N) converges to **~3.4 ns** for N ≥ 16K, which is ~9.4 clock cycles per comparison-swap on the Cortex core.

## Fair Comparison Methodology

All measurements use identical methodology:

1. **Same warmup**: 5 warmup runs before timing (both implementations)
2. **Same repeat count**: Median of 10 timed runs (both implementations)
3. **Same data range**: Full 32-bit `[0, 2³²-1]` uniform random integers (both implementations)
4. **Same timestamp stage**: `VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_ALL_COMMANDS_BIT` for all timestamps
5. **Same measurement type**: GPU timestamp envelope (first→last timestamp), not per-pass sum
6. **Same pipeline policy**: Vulkan pipeline created once, reused across all sizes
7. **Same frequency**: All 14 CPU cores locked to max frequency
8. **Correctness verified**: Each run verified against CPU `std::sort` result

### Remaining inherent differences

| Aspect | vulkan_radix_sort | VkRadixSort Multi |
|--------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Submit pattern | Single command buffer per sort | 4 command buffers, semaphore-chained |
| Dispatch count | 12 (3 × 4 passes) | 8 (2 × 4 passes) |
| Pipeline barriers | Between upsweep/spine/downsweep | Between histogram/scatter |
| Timestamp count | 2 (single envelope) | 8 (envelope from first to last) |

These are inherent to each algorithm's design and represent real-world performance characteristics.

- **SoC**: Kirin (ARM big.LITTLE, 14 cores)

## vulkan_radix_sort -- Dispatch Dimension Formulas

**Relevant source files:**
- `/home/huang/Graph/RadixSort/benchmark_repos/vulkan_radix_sort/include/vk_radix_sort.h` (lines 1004-1009 define constants, lines 1338-1492 contain the dispatch logic)
- `/home/huang/Graph/RadixSort/benchmark_repos/vulkan_radix_sort/src/shader/upsweep.comp`
- `/home/huang/Graph/RadixSort/benchmark_repos/vulkan_radix_sort/src/shader/spine.comp`
- `/home/huang/Graph/RadixSort/benchmark_repos/vulkan_radix_sort/src/shader/downsweep.comp`

**Constants (line 1004-1009):**
```cpp
constexpr uint32_t RADIX = 256;
constexpr int WORKGROUP_SIZE = 256;
constexpr int PARTITION_DIVISION = 8;
constexpr int PARTITION_SIZE = PARTITION_DIVISION * WORKGROUP_SIZE;  // = 2048
```

**Utility function (line 1009):**
```cpp
static uint32_t RoundUp(uint32_t a, uint32_t b) { return a / b + (a % b != 0); }
```

**Computed once per sort (line 1338):**
```cpp
uint32_t partitionCount = RoundUp(elementCount, PARTITION_SIZE);
```
That is: `partitionCount = ceil(N / 2048)`.

The sort runs 4 passes (one per byte). Each pass dispatches three shader stages:

1. **Upsweep** (line 1442):
   ```cpp
   vkCmdDispatch(commandBuffer, partitionCount, 1, 1);
   ```
   Dispatch X = `ceil(N / 2048)`. Each workgroup handles PARTITION_SIZE (2048) keys. The shader reads `gl_WorkGroupID.x` as its partition index, computes its own `partitionCount` from the element count buffer, and iterates over `RADIX = 256` bins to accumulate partition histograms.

2. **Spine** (line 1464-1465):
   ```cpp
   vkCmdDispatch(commandBuffer,
                 RoundUp(RADIX, WORKGROUP_SIZE / sorter->subgroupSize), 1, 1);
   ```
   Dispatch X = `ceil(256 / (256 / subgroupSize))` = `ceil(subgroupSize)`. On a device with `subgroupSize = 32`, this is `ceil(256 / 8) = 32` workgroups. On `subgroupSize = 64`, it is `ceil(256 / 4) = 64`. Each workgroup handles `WORKGROUP_SIZE / subgroupSize` radices (via waveIndex). The `subgroupSize` is queried from the device at sorter creation time. The spine shader is always a fixed-size dispatch -- it does **not** depend on N.

3. **Downsweep** (line 1492):
   ```cpp
   vkCmdDispatch(commandBuffer, partitionCount, 1, 1);
   ```
   Same as upsweep: Dispatch X = `ceil(N / 2048)`. The shader uses `gl_WorkGroupID.x` as `partitionIndex`, reads back the exclusive-prefix-summed partition histograms and global histograms, then scatters keys to their sorted positions.

---

## VkRadixSort -- Dispatch Dimension Formulas

**Relevant source files:**
- `/home/huang/Graph/RadixSort/benchmark_repos/VkRadixSort/singleradixsort/src/SingleRadixSort.cpp`
- `/home/huang/Graph/RadixSort/benchmark_repos/VkRadixSort/singleradixsort/resources/shaders/single_radixsort.comp`
- `/home/huang/Graph/RadixSort/benchmark_repos/VkRadixSort/multiradixsort/src/MultiRadixSort.cpp`
- `/home/huang/Graph/RadixSort/benchmark_repos/VkRadixSort/multiradixsort/resources/shaders/multi_radixsort_histograms.comp`
- `/home/huang/Graph/RadixSort/benchmark_repos/VkRadixSort/multiradixsort/resources/shaders/multi_radixsort.comp`
- `/home/huang/Graph/RadixSort/benchmark_repos/VkRadixSort/engine/include/engine/passes/ComputePass.h`

VkRadixSort has two implementations: a **single-pass** (single workgroup) and a **multi-pass** (multi-workgroup) variant.

### SingleRadixSort (single workgroup)

File: `SingleRadixSort.cpp` line 12:
```cpp
m_pass->setGlobalInvocationSize(SingleRadixSortPass::RADIX_SORT, 256, 1, 1);
```

This hard-codes 256 global invocations in X. The `ComputePass::setGlobalInvocationSize` method (ComputePass.h line 16-22) computes workgroup count as:
```cpp
dispatchSize.x = (width + workGroupSize.width - 1) / workGroupSize.width;
```
The shader has `local_size_x = 256`, so the dispatch is `ceil(256/256) = 1` workgroup.

The entire sort (4 iterations of histogram + scatter for 32-bit keys) runs in that single workgroup. The shader iterates over all elements in a loop (`for (uint ID = gl_LocalInvocationID.x; ID < g_num_elements; ID += WORKGROUP_SIZE)`).

### MultiRadixSort (multi-workgroup -- histogram + scatter passes)

This is the relevant one for the benchmark. It uses two shaders per pass: a **histograms** shader and a **scatter** shader.

File: `MultiRadixSort.cpp` lines 22-27:
```cpp
const uint32_t NUM_BLOCKS_PER_WORKGROUP = 32;
uint32_t globalInvocationSize = m_numElements / NUM_BLOCKS_PER_WORKGROUP;
uint32_t remainder = m_numElements % NUM_BLOCKS_PER_WORKGROUP;
globalInvocationSize += remainder > 0 ? 1 : 0;
m_pass->setGlobalInvocationSize(MultiRadixSortPass::RADIX_SORT_HISTOGRAMS, globalInvocationSize, 1, 1);
m_pass->setGlobalInvocationSize(MultiRadixSortPass::RADIX_SORT, globalInvocationSize, 1, 1);
```

The `globalInvocationSize` is passed as the "width" (total number of invocations) to `setGlobalInvocationSize`. Since the shader has `local_size_x = 256`, the actual workgroup count dispatched via `vkCmdDispatch` is:
```
workgroupCount = ceil(globalInvocationSize / 256)
             = ceil(ceil(N / 32) / 256)
             = ceil(N / 8192)
```

So both histogram and scatter dispatch the **same** number of workgroups: `ceil(N / 8192)`.

The push constants then communicate the actual workgroup count and elements-per-workgroup back to the shader:
```cpp
const uint32_t NUM_WORKGROUPS = m_pass->getWorkGroupCount(RADIX_SORT_HISTOGRAMS).width;
m_pass->m_pushConstantsHistogram.g_num_workgroups = NUM_WORKGROUPS;
m_pass->m_pushConstantsHistogram.g_num_blocks_per_workgroup = NUM_BLOCKS_PER_WORKGROUP;  // = 32
```

In the **histograms shader** (`multi_radixsort_histograms.comp`), each workgroup processes `g_num_blocks_per_workgroup * WORKGROUP_SIZE = 32 * 256 = 8192` elements via a loop (line 42):
```glsl
for (uint index = 0; index < g_num_blocks_per_workgroup; index++) {
    uint elementId = gl_WorkGroupID.x * g_num_blocks_per_workgroup * WORKGROUP_SIZE 
                     + index * WORKGROUP_SIZE + gl_LocalInvocationID.x;
```

In the **scatter shader** (`multi_radixsort.comp`), the same workgroup count is used. Each workgroup first reads the full histograms array (all `g_num_workgroups` workgroups' histograms) to compute global offsets via prefix sum, then scatters its own block of elements (lines 92-93):
```glsl
for (uint index = 0; index < g_num_blocks_per_workgroup; index++) {
    uint elementId = gl_WorkGroupID.x * g_num_blocks_per_workgroup * WORKGROUP_SIZE 
                     + index * WORKGROUP_SIZE + gl_LocalInvocationID.x;
```

| **vulkan_radix_sort** | Upsweep | `ceil(N / 2048)` | 2048 (PARTITION_SIZE) |
| **vulkan_radix_sort** | Spine | `ceil(256 / (256/subgroupSize))` = `subgroupSize` | Fixed (256 radix bins) |
| **vulkan_radix_sort** | Downsweep | `ceil(N / 2048)` | 2048 (PARTITION_SIZE) |

| **VkRadixSort** (Single) | Single pass | 1 | N (looped) |

VkRadixSort has two implementations: a **single-pass** (single workgroup) and a **multi-pass** (multi-workgroup) variant.

const uint32_t NUM_BLOCKS_PER_WORKGROUP = 32;

uint32_t remainder = m_numElements % NUM_BLOCKS_PER_WORKGROUP;

m_pass->setGlobalInvocationSize(MultiRadixSortPass::RADIX_SORT_HISTOGRAMS, globalInvocationSize, 1, 1);
m_pass->setGlobalInvocationSize(MultiRadixSortPass::RADIX_SORT, globalInvocationSize, 1, 1);
```

```

|---|---|---|

| **Upsweep/Histogram WG** | `ceil(N / 2048)` | `ceil(N / 8192)` |
| **Spine WG** | `subgroupSize` = 32 (固定) | — |
| **Downsweep/Scatter WG** | `ceil(N / 2048)` | `ceil(N / 8192)` |

| **总 dispatch 数** | 12 (3×4) | 8 (2×4) |

| N | vrs WG/pass (upsweep+downsweep) | vrs Spine WG | vkr WG/pass (hist+scatter) | vrs 总 WG | vkr 总 WG |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1K | 1 | 32 | 1 | 34 | 2 |
| 32K | 16 | 32 | 4 | 64 | 8 |
| 1M | 512 | 32 | 128 | 1056 | 256 |
| 2M | 1024 | 32 | 256 | 2080 | 512 |
| 4M | 2048 | 32 | 512 | 4128 | 1024 |
| 8M | 4096 | 32 | 1024 | 8224 | 2048 |

**核心差异：**

1. **vrs 的 workgroup 粒度更细**（2048 vs 8192 元素/WG），意味着更多并行度。在 1M 时 vrs 发射 512 个 WG 而 vkr 只发射 128 个 — vrs 对 GPU SM 的填充率更高。

2. **vrs 多了一个 spine pass**（固定 32 个 WG），但这只做全局直方图的前缀和（256 个 bin），开销极小。

## 1. GPU 占用率：WG 少 → SM 吃不饱

content.text:
现在可以做精确对比了。关键在于 **scatter/downsweep 阶段的算法复杂度**差异：

## 性能影响分析

### 影响 1：vkr scatter 的 O(num_WG) 全局内存读取（最大瓶颈）

vkr scatter shader 第 56-63 行：

```glsl
// 每个 workgroup 都要读 ALL workgroups 的直方图
for (uint j = 0; j < g_num_workgroups; j++) {
    const uint t = g_histograms[256 * j + binID];  // 全局内存！
    histogram_count += t;
}
```

这是**全局内存读取**，不是共享内存。每个 workgroup 的前 256 个线程各读 `g_num_workgroups` 个 uint：

| N | g_num_workgroups | 全局内存读取量 (per WG) | 总读取量 (all WGs) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1M | 128 | 128 KB | 16 MB |
| 4M | 512 | 512 KB | 256 MB |
| **8M** | **1024** | **1 MB** | **1 GB** |

**8M 时 scatter 的前缀和阶段就读了 1 GB 全局内存**，这远超排序本身的数据量（8M × 4B = 32 MB）。这就是 4M→8M 断崖式退化的根本原因。

### 影响 2：vrs 用独立 spine pass 避免了这个问题

vrs 的 downsweep 第 165-169 行：

```glsl
// 直接读预计算好的全局直方图，O(1) 读取
localHistogramSum[i] = globalHistogram[...] + partitionHistogram[...] - localHistogramSum[i];
```

vrs 的全局前缀和由**独立的 spine dispatch** 完成（固定 32 个 WG），downsweep 只需 O(1) 读取预计算结果。代价是多了一次 dispatch，但完全消除了 O(num_WG) 的扩展问题。

### 影响 3：vkr scatter 的 bin_flags 共享内存开销

scatter 阶段的排序（第 92-135 行），每个 block 需要：

```
shared BinFlags[256]  →  256 × (256/32) × 4 = 256 × 8 × 4 = 8 KB
```

加上 `global_offsets[256]` = 1 KB，共 **9 KB 共享内存/WG**。每个 block 都要初始化 + barrier + 读取这 8 KB 的 bin_flags。WG 内有 `g_num_blocks_per_workgroup = 32` 个 block，所以这个初始化-读取循环跑 32 次。

而 vrs downsweep 用 **subgroup ballot** 替代 bin_flags：

```glsl
uvec4 mask = subgroupBallot(true);
for (uint bit = 0; bit < 8; ++bit) {
    uvec4 ballot = subgroupBallot(digit == 1u);
    mask &= uvec4(digit - 1u) ^ ballot;
}
uint waveOffset = getBitCount(waveMask & mask);
```

这是**硬件级并行排名**，零共享内存开销，zero barrier。8 个 ballot 指令 vs 8 KB 共享内存的初始化+遍历。

### 总结

| 因素 | vrs | vkr | 影响 |
|------|-----|-----|------|
| 全局前缀和 | 独立 spine pass，固定 32 WG | scatter 内 O(num_WG) 读取 | **8M 时 vkr 多读 1 GB** |
| WG 内排名 | subgroup ballot（硬件） | bin_flags 8 KB shared memory | vrs 零额外内存 |
| Atomics | wave 内仅 waveOffset==0 时 1 次 | 每元素 atomicAdd | vrs 少 ~32× atomics |
| WG 粒度 | 2048 elem/WG | 8192 elem/WG | vrs 更好的 GPU 填充率 |
| Dispatch 开销 | 12 次 | 8 次 | vkr 小 N 时有优势 |

**根本原因**：vkr 的设计假设 workgroup 数量不会太大（`for j in 0..g_num_workgroups`），当数据量增长到需要上千个 workgroup 时，scatter 的全局内存读取变成了主导开销。vrs 通过将全局前缀和抽成独立的 spine pass，彻底避免了这个扩展性问题。

# HarmonyOS Maleoon 935 Vulkan Notes

Date verified: 2026-05-28

## Context

This repo was cross-compiled with the HarmonyOS native SDK and tested on a HarmonyOS arm64 phone with a Maleoon 935 Vulkan device.

The original desktop-oriented shader configuration used `WORKGROUP_SIZE = 512`. On Maleoon 935, that configuration created compute pipelines successfully but lost the Vulkan device during queue execution.

Observed failure signature:

```text
vkQueueSubmit result=0
vkWaitForFences wait=-4
```

`-4` is `VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST`. The first GPU output value also stayed equal to the unsorted input value, while the CPU reference path passed.

## Key compatibility change

Use `WORKGROUP_SIZE = 256` for HarmonyOS/Maleoon compatibility.

Files that must stay consistent:

- `src/shader/upsweep.comp`
- `src/shader/spine.comp`
- `src/shader/downsweep.comp`
- `src/shader/constants.slang`
- `src/vk_radix_sort.h.in`
- regenerated `include/vk_radix_sort.h`

Do not change only one shader file. The host-side `PARTITION_SIZE` calculation and all shader-local constants must match.

## Required synchronization for the benchmark

The HarmonyOS device exposed host/device synchronization assumptions that were implicit in the benchmark. Desktop platforms may hide these issues because of memory type choices, driver behavior, or queue submission behavior, but the mobile path needs them to be explicit.

### 1. Flush after host writes to the staging buffer

`bench/vulkan_benchmark.cc` uses a mapped staging buffer to pass CPU-generated input data to the GPU. The host-side `std::memcpy()` only writes to the CPU-visible mapped address. It does not guarantee that those writes are immediately visible to GPU transfer reads.

Before submitting `vkCmdCopyBuffer(staging -> device buffer)`, call:

```cpp
vmaFlushAllocation(allocator_, staging_.allocation, 0, size);
```

The keys-only path flushes `inout_size`. The key-value path flushes `2 * inout_size + sizeof(uint32_t)`, because the same staging buffer contains keys, values, and the indirect element count.

Without this flush, the GPU can read stale or unflushed input data, which shows up as output mismatches against the CPU reference.

### 2. Invalidate before host reads from the staging buffer

After sorting, the benchmark uses `vkCmdCopyBuffer(device buffer -> staging)` to copy results back into the mapped staging buffer. Even after the GPU write has completed, directly reading the mapped address with `std::memcpy()` does not guarantee the host sees the latest contents.

Before the host reads the staging buffer, call:

```cpp
vmaInvalidateAllocation(allocator_, staging_.allocation, 0, size);
```

The keys-only path invalidates `inout_size`. The key-value path invalidates `2 * inout_size`.

Without this invalidate, the CPU can read old contents from before the copy-back. During debugging, the first GPU output value was observed to remain equal to the original unsorted input value, which is the kind of symptom missing invalidate or copy-back visibility can produce.

### 3. Add a barrier between upload transfer and sort dispatch

Input data is first written into GPU buffers by a transfer copy, then read by compute shaders during sorting. Even if the copy and sort are submitted separately and waited on with fences, the benchmark should still express the resource dependency explicitly: transfer writes must be visible before shader reads.

The pre-sort barrier is:

```cpp
VkMemoryBarrier sort_before = {VK_STRUCTURE_TYPE_MEMORY_BARRIER};
sort_before.srcAccessMask = VK_ACCESS_TRANSFER_WRITE_BIT;
sort_before.dstAccessMask = VK_ACCESS_SHADER_READ_BIT;
vkCmdPipelineBarrier(commandBuffer,
                     VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_TRANSFER_BIT,
                     VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_COMPUTE_SHADER_BIT,
                     0, 1, &sort_before, 0, nullptr, 0, nullptr);
```

The key-value indirect path also lets the sort command read the indirect element count, so the destination access mask needs to cover both shader reads and transfer reads:

```cpp
sort_before.dstAccessMask = VK_ACCESS_SHADER_READ_BIT | VK_ACCESS_TRANSFER_READ_BIT;
```

### 4. Add a barrier between sort dispatch and copy-back transfer

The sort dispatch writes output buffers through compute shaders, and the benchmark immediately copies those results back to staging through a transfer copy. This must explicitly express that shader writes are visible before transfer reads.

The pre-copy-back barrier is:

```cpp
VkMemoryBarrier sort_after = {VK_STRUCTURE_TYPE_MEMORY_BARRIER};
sort_after.srcAccessMask = VK_ACCESS_SHADER_WRITE_BIT;
sort_after.dstAccessMask = VK_ACCESS_TRANSFER_READ_BIT;
vkCmdPipelineBarrier(commandBuffer,
                     VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_COMPUTE_SHADER_BIT,
                     VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_TRANSFER_BIT,
                     0, 1, &sort_after, 0, nullptr, 0, nullptr);
```

Without this barrier, the copy-back transfer can read the buffer before shader writes are visible to the transfer stage, causing the host to see unsorted or partially updated data.

### 5. These sync points are benchmark boundaries

The `vk_radix_sort` library already inserts internal barriers between compute passes such as upsweep, spine, and downsweep. The synchronization described here is external synchronization around the benchmark's use of the library:

- The boundary from host staging writes to GPU input buffers.
- The boundary from GPU sort output to host staging reads.

When integrating the library into another project, callers still need equivalent synchronization around their own resource flow. Do not assume the library function handles every producer/consumer relationship for external buffers.

These synchronization steps are implemented in `bench/vulkan_benchmark.cc` for both the keys-only and key-value paths.

## Verified build command

```bash
cmake -S benchmark_repos/vulkan_radix_sort \
  -B benchmark_repos/vulkan_radix_sort/build-ohos-arm64 \
  -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE="$HOME/harmonyos/linux/native/build/cmake/ohos.toolchain.cmake" \
  -DOHOS_ARCH=arm64-v8a \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DBENCH_ENABLE_EMBREE_CUDA=OFF \
  -DVulkan_INCLUDE_DIR="$HOME/harmonyos/linux/native/sysroot/usr/include" \
  -DVulkan_LIBRARY="$HOME/harmonyos/linux/native/sysroot/usr/lib/aarch64-linux-ohos/libvulkan.so" \
  -DVulkan_GLSLANG_VALIDATOR_EXECUTABLE=/usr/bin/glslangValidator

cmake --build benchmark_repos/vulkan_radix_sort/build-ohos-arm64 --target bench -j
```

## Verified deploy and run commands

```bash
$HOME/harmonyos/linux/toolchains/hdc shell "mkdir -p /data/local/tmp/vulkan_radix_sort"
$HOME/harmonyos/linux/toolchains/hdc file send \
  benchmark_repos/vulkan_radix_sort/build-ohos-arm64/bench \
  /data/local/tmp/vulkan_radix_sort/bench
$HOME/harmonyos/linux/toolchains/hdc shell \
  "chmod 755 /data/local/tmp/vulkan_radix_sort/bench"

$HOME/harmonyos/linux/toolchains/hdc shell \
  "cd /data/local/tmp/vulkan_radix_sort && ./bench vulkan /data/local/tmp/vulkan_radix_sort/vulkan_clean_1024.csv 1024"

$HOME/harmonyos/linux/toolchains/hdc shell \
  "cd /data/local/tmp/vulkan_radix_sort && ./bench vulkan /data/local/tmp/vulkan_radix_sort/vulkan_clean_1m.csv 1048576"
```

## Regression checklist

Before treating future HarmonyOS/Maleoon changes as working:

1. Rebuild `bench` with the HarmonyOS toolchain.
2. Push the binary to `/data/local/tmp/vulkan_radix_sort/bench`.
3. Run Vulkan correctness at `N=1024`.
4. Run Vulkan correctness at `N=1048576`.
5. Confirm neither run reports `VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST` or a correctness failure.

## Device info

- **SoC**: Kirin (ARM big.LITTLE)
- **CPU topology**: 4×1.53 GHz (LITTLE) + 8×2.10 GHz (mid) + 2×2.75 GHz (big)
- **GPU**: Maleoon 935, Vulkan 1.4.309
- **subgroupSize**: 32, maxComputeInvocations=1024, maxSharedMemory=32768
- **timestampPeriod**: ~107 ns/tick (must multiply GPU raw tick differences by this value)

## Performance results

See [BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md](BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md) for the full GPU vs CPU benchmark data.

content.thinking:
The user is asking me to think about whether DVFS (Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling) would affect the benchmark results, before actually locking the DDR frequency. This is a great question - let me think through all the DVFS domains that could affect GPU benchmark results on this device.

On a mobile SoC like Kirin with Maleoon 935, there are several DVFS domains:

1. **CPU DVFS** - Already locked (all 14 cores locked to max freq)
2. **GPU DVFS** - The GPU itself has its own frequency scaling
3. **DDR/Memory DVFS** - Memory bus frequency scaling
4. **Bus/Interconnect DVFS** - Bus frequency scaling
5. **GPU power state** - GPU may have power gating states

Let me think about which ones matter for GPU radix sort benchmarking:

### GPU DVFS
The GPU itself may be scaling its frequency based on workload. This is critical - if the GPU is running at a lower frequency during small N tests and ramping up for large N tests, the results would be distorted. The warmup runs help with this, but may not fully stabilize GPU frequency.

How to check/lock:
- `/sys/class/devfreq/` - look for GPU device
- Or `/sys/devices/platform/.../gpu/` or similar vendor-specific paths
- Or the Vulkan driver might have its own power management

### DDR/Memory DVFS
DDR frequency directly affects memory bandwidth, which is the critical bottleneck for radix sort (especially scatter-heavy workloads). If DDR frequency changes between runs or during a single run, results would be inconsistent.

This is especially relevant because:
- Our analysis showed VkRadixSort's scatter kernel does O(num_WG) global memory reads
- At 8M, this is 1 GB of global memory reads - very memory bandwidth sensitive
- If DDR frequency drops mid-benchmark, it would amplify the degradation we see

### Bus/Interconnect DVFS
Similar to DDR - if the bus between GPU and memory scales frequency, it affects bandwidth.

### GPU Power States
The GPU might be in a low-power state initially and take time to ramp up. The 5 warmup runs help, but if there's a long idle period between benchmark sizes, the GPU might power down again.

Let me think about what we should recommend:

1. **Check all DVFS domains** - List all devfreq devices
2. **Lock GPU frequency** - This is probably the most important one we haven't locked yet!
3. **Lock DDR frequency** - Important for memory-bound workloads
4. **Lock bus frequency** - If applicable
5. **Disable GPU power gating** - Keep GPU awake between tests

Actually, wait - we locked CPU frequency but did we lock GPU frequency? Looking back at the summary, it says "All 14 CPU cores locked to max via scaling_min_freq = scaling_max_freq" - this is CPU only! We never locked GPU frequency!

This is a significant omission. The GPU could be running at different frequencies depending on:
- Thermal throttling
- Workload detection
- Power budget

Let me also think about DVFS effects on our specific findings:

1. The "VkRadixSort degrades at 4M→8M" finding - could this be affected by DVFS? If the GPU hits a thermal limit during the 8M test, it might throttle, making the degradation look worse than it actually is. But the fact that vulkan_radix_sort doesn't show similar degradation (58ms is well-behaved) suggests this isn't thermal throttling of the GPU itself - it's more likely memory pressure.

2. However, if DDR frequency drops under load (memory controller thermal throttling), that would affect VkRadixSort more because it does more memory reads.

3. The 5 warmup runs might stabilize GPU frequency for the first size, but between sizes there might be idle periods where DVFS scales down.

Let me provide a thorough analysis of all DVFS domains that could affect the results.

python3 << 'PYEOF'
# Let's think through all DVFS domains systematically

analysis = """
# DVFS 域对 GPU Radix Sort Benchmark 的影响分析

## 已锁定的 DVFS 域
✅ CPU 频率 — 14 个核全部锁到 max (scaling_min_freq = scaling_max_freq)

## 未锁定的 DVFS 域（可能有影响）

### 1. GPU 自身频率 (GPU DVFS) ⚠️⚠️⚠️ 最关键
- GPU 有自己的频率调节，通常在 /sys/class/devfreq/ 下
- warmup 5 次可能把 GPU 频率拉上来，但：
  a) 不同 N 之间如果间隔长，GPU 可能降频
  b) 大负载（8M）时可能触发热 throttling 降频
  c) 小 N 时 GPU 可能不需要高频就能完成

### 2. DDR 内存频率 (DDR DVFS) ⚠️⚠️ 关键
- DDR 频率直接影响显存带宽
- radix sort 是内存密集型：
  - vrs 8M keys: 读 32MB + 写 32MB × 4 passes ≈ 256 MB
  - vkr 8M scatter: 额外读 1 GB 直方图前缀和
- DDR 降频对 vkr 影响远大于 vrs（因为 vkr 的内存读取量远大）
- 如果 DDR 在大负载时降频，会放大 vkr 的退化

### 3. 总线/互连频率 (Bus DVFS) ⚠️
- GPU↔内存的总线频率
- 影响同 DDR，内存带宽的一部分

### 4. GPU 电源状态 (Power Gating)
- GPU 空闲时可能进入低功耗状态
- 唤醒延迟可能影响第一个 benchmark size
- warmup 应该解决了这个问题

## 需要排查的关键问题

Q1: GPU 频率是否在所有 benchmark runs 中保持稳定？
   → 没有 GPU 频率监控数据，无法确认
   → 当前 warmup 可能把频率拉上来，但不能排除 throttling

### 2. DDR 内存频率 (DDR DVFS) ⚠️⚠️ 关键

content.text:
## DVFS 对性能测试的影响分析

### 我们当前只锁了 CPU，遗漏了三个关键 DVFS 域

| DVFS 域 | 状态 | 影响程度 | 说明 |
|---------|------|----------|------|
| CPU 频率 | ✅ 已锁 | — | 14 核全锁 max |
| **GPU 频率** | ❌ 未锁 | ⚠️⚠️⚠️ | 最关键，直接影响所有 GPU 计算时间 |
| **DDR 频率** | ❌ 未锁 | ⚠️⚠️ | 影响内存带宽，vkr scatter 尤其敏感 |
| **总线频率** | ❌ 未锁 | ⚠️ | GPU↔内存互连带宽 |

### 核心问题：GPU 频率可能比 DDR 更重要

我们一直没锁 GPU 频率。这意味着：

1. **GPU 可能在不同 N 下跑不同频率** — 小 N 时 GPU 可能认为负载低而降频，导致 GPU latency floor 偏高
2. **大 N 可能触发热 throttling** — 连续跑 8M × 4 passes × 15 runs = 480M 元素排序，GPU 可能已经过热降频
3. **warmup 只解决冷启动，不解决 throttling** — warmup 把频率拉上来，但持续高负载可能让 GPU 反而降下去

### 对当前结论的影响

**关键判断**：8M 时 vkr 的 2.96× 退化是算法问题还是 DVFS？

- **vrs 8M 只增长 1.60×**（正常），说明 GPU 没有整体降频
- 但如果 **DDR 在重载时降频**（内存控制器热 throttling），vkr 受影响更大因为它做了 1 GB 的全局内存读取（vrs 只做了 256 MB）
- 所以：退化可能是 **算法问题 + DDR DVFS 叠加**

### 连接手机后需要做的事

```bash
# 1. 列出所有 devfreq 设备
hdc shell "ls -la /sys/class/devfreq/"

# 2. 查看每个设备的 governor、当前频率、可用频率
hdc shell "for d in /sys/class/devfreq/*/; do \
  echo '=== '$d; \
  cat \$d/governor_name 2>/dev/null; \
  cat \$d/cur_freq 2>/dev/null; \
  cat \$d/max_freq 2>/dev/null; \
  cat \$d/min_freq 2>/dev/null; \
  cat \$d/available_frequencies 2>/dev/null; \
done"

# 3. 特别关注 GPU 和 DDR
# GPU 通常在 /sys/class/devfreq/ 下有 "gpu" 或 "mali" 或 "maleoon" 关键字
# DDR 通常有 "ddr" / "dmc" / "mem" / "bus" 关键字

# 4. 锁频方案
# GPU: echo performance > governor  或  min_freq = max_freq
# DDR: 同上
# Bus: 同上
```

连上手机后把 `ls /sys/class/devfreq/` 的结果贴给我，我来帮你确认哪些是 GPU/DDR/Bus 并给出锁频命令。

'

结果非常有意义。锁频后几个关键发现：

### 锁频的巨大影响

**之前 DVFS 自动模式下 GPU 基本没跑满：**
- 小 N（1K-64K）：vrs 快了 **2.3-3.2×**，vkr 快了 **1.4-4.2×**
- 大 N（8M）：vrs 只快了 **1.02×**（说明之前 DVFS 在大负载时已经把频率拉上去了）
- **GPU latency floor 从 ~0.7ms 降到了 ~0.29ms**（之前 GPU 在 235 MHz 空转）

### 锁频后的关键变化

**1. vkr 8M 退化仍然存在但变小了：**
- DVFS auto: 4M→8M 增长 **2.96×** 
- 全锁频: 4M→8M 增长 **3.43×**（甚至更大！）
- 说明退化**不是** DDR throttling 导致的，是算法本身的问题

**2. vrs 的 GPU latency floor 从 0.7ms 降到 0.29ms：**
- 8K 时 vrs 就已经超过 CPU（1.13×），比之前的 32K 交叉点大幅提前

**3. vrs 的吞吐量在 1M 就已经接近饱和（139 MItems/s），到 8M 仅微增到 147 MItems/s**

input.content:
# Radix Sort Benchmark Results — Maleoon 935

Date: 2026-06-11

## Test Environment

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| **Device** | HarmonyOS arm64 phone |
| **GPU** | Maleoon 935, Vulkan 1.4.309, subgroupSize=32 |
| **GPU freq** | Locked 933 MHz (max), was 235 MHz idle / DVFS auto |
| **DDR freq** | Locked 4800 MHz (max), was 1066 MHz idle / DVFS auto |
| **L1 bus freq** | Locked 1172 MHz (max) |
| **CPU** | Kirin big.LITTLE: 4×1.72 GHz + 8×2.27 GHz + 2×2.75 GHz |
| **CPU freq** | All 14 cores locked to max |
| **CPU sort** | `std::sort` / `std::stable_sort`, pinned to big cores (cpu12-13, 2.75 GHz) |
| **GPU timing** | `vkCmdWriteTimestamp` (ALL_COMMANDS_BIT) × `timestampPeriod` (~107 ns/tick), envelope |
| **CPU timing** | `std::chrono::high_resolution_clock` for `std::sort` |
| **Build** | HarmonyOS NDK cross-compiled, `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` |
| **Sizes** | 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K, 32K, 64K, 128K, 256K, 512K, 1M, 2M, 4M, 8M |

## DVFS Locking

All DVFS domains locked to maximum frequency via sysfs:

```
GPU:  echo 933000000  > /sys/class/devfreq/gpufreq/{min,max}_freq        (235 → 933 MHz)
DDR:  echo 4800000000 > /sys/class/devfreq/ddrfreq/{min,max}_freq        (1066 → 4800 MHz)
DDRL: echo 4800000000 > /sys/class/devfreq/ddrfreq_latency/{min,max}_freq
BUS:  echo 1172000000 > /sys/class/devfreq/ddrfreq_l1bus_latency/{min,max}_freq
CPU:  echo $max_freq   > /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_min_freq
```

DVFS auto mode had GPU running at 235 MHz (25% of max) and DDR at 1066 MHz (22% of max) during idle. Locking all domains removes frequency as a variable, making measurements deterministic and reproducible.

## Algorithms Compared

| Algorithm | Source | Dispatch/Pass | Pipeline | Warmup | Runs |
|-----------|--------|---------------|----------|--------|------|
| **CPU std::sort** | C++ STL | — | — | 5 | 10 (median) |
| **vulkan_radix_sort** | [vulkan_radix_sort](.) | 3 dispatch/pass (upsweep→spine→downsweep) × 4 passes | Created once | 5 | 10 (median) |
| **VkRadixSort Multi** | [VkRadixSort](../VkRadixSort) | 2 dispatch/pass (histogram→scatter) × 4 passes | Created once (reused) | 5 | 10 (median) |

Both GPU radix sorts operate on 32-bit unsigned integers (full range `[0, 2³²-1]`) with 4 × 8-bit radix passes and `WORKGROUP_SIZE=256`.

## Timing Methodology

Both GPU implementations use `vkCmdWriteTimestamp` with `VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_ALL_COMMANDS_BIT` to measure the **envelope** time from first to last timestamp:

- **vulkan_radix_sort**: 2 timestamps (start/end) around the entire sort command buffer → single envelope
- **VkRadixSort Multi**: 8 timestamps (2 per iteration × 4 iterations) → envelope from first to last timestamp

This captures the full GPU pipeline including barriers, fill buffer, and inter-dispatch synchronization, making the measurements directly comparable.

## Full Comparison (All Frequencies Locked)

![Three-way comparison](benchmark_comparison_full.png)

### Keys-only Sort (GPU timestamp envelope, median of 10 runs)

| N | CPU (ms) | vulkan_radix_sort (ms) | VkRadixSort Multi (ms) | vrs/CPU | vkr/CPU | vkr/vrs |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1K | 0.038 | 0.287 | 0.392 | 0.13× | 0.10× | 1.37× |
| 2K | 0.076 | 0.295 | 0.417 | 0.26× | 0.18× | 1.41× |
| 4K | 0.167 | 0.298 | 0.473 | 0.56× | 0.35× | 1.59× |
| **8K** | **0.349** | **0.308** | **0.547** | **1.13×** | 0.64× | 1.78× |
| **16K** | **0.768** | **0.311** | **0.620** | **2.47×** | **1.24×** | 1.99× |
| **32K** | **1.641** | **0.442** | **0.566** | **3.71×** | **2.90×** | 1.28× |
| 64K | 3.503 | 0.610 | 0.865 | 5.74× | 4.05× | 1.42× |
| 128K | 7.511 | 1.104 | 1.317 | 6.80× | 5.70× | 1.19× |
| 256K | 15.977 | 2.153 | 2.403 | 7.42× | 6.65× | 1.12× |
| 512K | 33.768 | 3.936 | 4.631 | 8.58× | 7.29× | 1.18× |
| **1M** | **71.216** | **7.535** | **9.254** | **9.45×** | **7.70×** | 1.23× |
| **2M** | **150.964** | **14.713** | **19.042** | **10.26×** | **7.93×** | 1.29× |
| **4M** | **317.808** | **28.725** | **38.705** | **11.06×** | **8.21×** | 1.35× |
| **8M** | **684.130** | **57.050** | **132.641** | **11.99×** | **5.16×** | **2.32×** |

> **vrs/CPU** = CPU time / vulkan_radix_sort time (>1 = GPU faster)
> **vkr/CPU** = CPU time / VkRadixSort time (>1 = GPU faster)
> **vkr/vrs** = VkRadixSort time / vulkan_radix_sort time (>1 = vulkan_radix_sort faster, <1 = VkRadixSort faster)

### Key-Value Sort (vulkan_radix_sort only)

| N | CPU kv (ms) | vrs kv GPU (ms) | GPU Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1K | 0.053 | 0.316 | 0.17× |
| 2K | 0.117 | 0.328 | 0.36× |
| 4K | 0.220 | 0.330 | 0.67× |
| 8K | 0.511 | 0.332 | 1.54× |
| **16K** | **1.018** | **0.360** | **2.83×** |
| **32K** | **2.379** | **0.526** | **4.52×** |
| 64K | 4.859 | 0.777 | 6.25× |
| 128K | 11.114 | 1.468 | 7.57× |
| 256K | 22.340 | 3.095 | 7.22× |
| 512K | 50.696 | 5.693 | 8.90× |
| **1M** | **105.247** | **10.984** | **9.58×** |
| **2M** | **246.798** | **21.543** | **11.46×** |
| **4M** | **528.225** | **42.898** | **12.31×** |
| **8M** | **1249.504** | **85.528** | **14.61×** |

### Scaling Curves

![Scaling comparison](benchmark_comparison_scaling.png)

## Key Findings

### 1. DVFS Locking Impact

Locking GPU (235→933 MHz) and DDR (1066→4800 MHz) dramatically changed results:

| Metric | DVFS Auto | All Locked | Change |
|--------|----------:|-----------:|-------:|
| vrs GPU latency floor | ~0.7 ms | **~0.29 ms** | 2.4× lower |
| vrs 1M | 16.1 ms | **7.5 ms** | 2.1× faster |
| vrs 8M | 58.2 ms | **57.0 ms** | 1.02× (already at max) |
| vkr 1M | 20.3 ms | **9.3 ms** | 2.2× faster |
| vkr 8M | 147.2 ms | **132.6 ms** | 1.1× faster |

Key insight: Under DVFS auto, the GPU was at 25% frequency (235 MHz) during small-N tests. Large-N tests naturally ramped up frequency, making earlier data appear to show better GPU scaling than actually exists.

### 2. Crossover Points

| Algorithm | Crossover N | Speedup at Crossover |
|-----------|:-----------:|:--------------------:|
| vulkan_radix_sort | **8K** | 1.13× |
| VkRadixSort Multi | **16K** | 1.24× |

With frequencies locked, crossover drops from 32K/64K to **8K/16K** — the GPU is useful at much smaller sizes than DVFS-auto data suggested.

### 3. vulkan_radix_sort vs VkRadixSort Multi

| Size Range | vkr/vrs | Winner | Margin |
|------------|:-------:|--------|--------|
| 1K–2K | 1.37–1.41× | vulkan_radix_sort | 37–41% |
| 4K | 1.59× | vulkan_radix_sort | 59% |
| 8K–16K | 1.78–1.99× | vulkan_radix_sort | 78–99% |
| 32K | 1.28× | vulkan_radix_sort | 28% |
| 64K–256K | 1.12–1.42× | vulkan_radix_sort | 12–42% |
| 512K–4M | 1.18–1.35× | vulkan_radix_sort | 18–35% |
| **8M** | **2.32×** | **vulkan_radix_sort** | **132%** |

vulkan_radix_sort wins at **all sizes** with all frequencies locked. The gap is smallest at 256K (1.12×) and widest at 16K (1.99×) and 8M (2.32×).

### 4. Peak Performance (N=8M, All Locked)

| Sort | GPU (ms) | CPU (ms) | GPU Speedup | Throughput |
|------|--------:|--------:|------------:|-----------:|
| **vulkan_radix_sort keys** | 57.05 | 684.13 | **11.99×** | **147 MItems/s** |
| **vulkan_radix_sort kv** | 85.53 | 1249.50 | **14.61×** | 98 MItems/s |
| VkRadixSort Multi keys | 132.64 | 684.13 | 5.16× | 63 MItems/s |
| CPU std::sort | — | 684.13 | 1.00× | 12 MItems/s |

### 5. Scaling Analysis

How time grows when data doubles (ideal = 2.00×):

### Scaling Curves

![Scaling comparison](benchmark_comparison_scaling.png)

## Key Findings

### 1. Crossover Points

| Algorithm | Crossover N | Speedup at Crossover |
|-----------|:-----------:|:--------------------:|
| vulkan_radix_sort | **32K** | 1.18× |
| VkRadixSort Multi | **64K** | 1.06× |

At N < 32K, CPU `std::sort` is faster due to GPU launch overhead (~0.7 ms latency floor).

### 2. vulkan_radix_sort vs VkRadixSort Multi

| Size Range | vkr/vrs | Winner | Margin |
|------------|:-------:|--------|--------|
| 1K | 0.64× | **VkRadixSort** | 36% |
| 2K | 0.83× | VkRadixSort | 17% |
| 4K | 1.20× | vulkan_radix_sort | 20% |
| 8K–16K | 1.56–1.62× | vulkan_radix_sort | 56–62% |
| 32K–64K | 1.68–1.76× | vulkan_radix_sort | 68–76% |
| 128K–512K | 1.34–1.91× | vulkan_radix_sort | 34–91% |
| 1M | 1.26× | vulkan_radix_sort | 26% |
| 2M | 1.63× | vulkan_radix_sort | 63% |
| 4M | 1.37× | vulkan_radix_sort | 37% |
| **8M** | **2.53×** | **vulkan_radix_sort** | **153%** |

**VkRadixSort wins at N ≤ 2K** where its lower dispatch count (2 vs 3 per pass) gives it a latency advantage. At N ≥ 4K, vulkan_radix_sort wins consistently. The gap widens dramatically at N=8M where VkRadixSort suffers memory pressure (2.96× growth for 2× data from 4M→8M).

### 3. Peak Performance (N=8M, Locked)

| Sort | GPU (ms) | CPU (ms) | GPU Speedup | Throughput |
|------|--------:|--------:|------------:|-----------:|
| **vulkan_radix_sort keys** | 58.25 | 680.44 | **11.68×** | **144 MItems/s** |
| **vulkan_radix_sort kv** | 83.89 | 1237.92 | **14.76×** | 100 MItems/s |
| VkRadixSort Multi keys | 147.24 | 680.44 | 4.62× | 57 MItems/s |
| CPU std::sort | — | 680.44 | 1.00× | 12 MItems/s |

### 4. Scaling Analysis

How time grows when data doubles (ideal = 2.00×):

| Transition | CPU | vulkan_radix_sort | VkRadixSort |
|:----------:|:---:|:-----------------:|:-----------:|
| 1M → 2M | 2.09× | **1.38×** | 1.79× |
| 2M → 4M | 2.11× | **1.64×** | 1.37× |
| 4M → 8M | 2.14× | **1.60×** | **2.96×** ⚠️ |

**vulkan_radix_sort scales sub-linearly** at large N — its throughput keeps climbing (65 → 94 → 115 → 144 MItems/s) as the GPU becomes more utilized. At N=8M it reaches **144 MItems/s**, 2.5× its throughput at 1M.

**VkRadixSort degrades at 4M→8M**: time grows 2.96× for 2× data, and throughput drops from 84 to 57 MItems/s. This is likely caused by memory pressure — at 8M, the keys buffer (32 MB) + ping-pong buffer + histograms approach or exceed available GPU memory, and VkRadixSort's scatter-based random write pattern suffers high cache/TLB miss rates.

### 5. CPU Scaling

CPU `std::sort` at locked 2.75 GHz follows O(N log N) exactly. The normalized time T/(N·log₂N) converges to **~3.4 ns** for N ≥ 16K, which is ~9.4 clock cycles per comparison-swap on the Cortex core.

### 6. Why the Gap Widens at Large N

The two implementations use fundamentally different scatter strategies:

| Aspect | vulkan_radix_sort (downsweep) | VkRadixSort (scatter) |
|--------|-------------------------------|----------------------|
| Atomics | `subgroupBallot` for wave-internal ranking; 1 `atomicAdd` per radix bin only when `waveOffset==0` | `atomicAdd(histogram[bin], 1U)` in shared memory per element |
| Scatter reads | Direct partition-based output | 8×256 shared memory reads per element via `bin_flags` |
| Prefix sum | Single global histogram per pass | Per-workgroup histograms → prefix sum over ALL workgroups |
| Memory pattern | Better locality (partition-based) | Random write scatter |

At small N, VkRadixSort's lower dispatch count (8 vs 12 total) gives it an edge. At large N, vulkan_radix_sort's more efficient atomics and better memory locality dominate.

## Fair Comparison Methodology

All measurements use identical methodology:

1. **Same warmup**: 5 warmup runs before timing (both implementations)
2. **Same repeat count**: Median of 10 timed runs (both implementations)
3. **Same data range**: Full 32-bit `[0, 2³²-1]` uniform random integers (both implementations)
4. **Same timestamp stage**: `VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_ALL_COMMANDS_BIT` for all timestamps
5. **Same measurement type**: GPU timestamp envelope (first→last timestamp), not per-pass sum
6. **Same pipeline policy**: Vulkan pipeline created once, reused across all sizes
7. **Same frequency**: All 14 CPU cores locked to max frequency
8. **Correctness verified**: Each run verified against CPU `std::sort` result

### Remaining inherent differences

| Aspect | vulkan_radix_sort | VkRadixSort Multi |
|--------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Submit pattern | Single command buffer per sort | 4 command buffers, semaphore-chained |
| Dispatch count | 12 (3 × 4 passes) | 8 (2 × 4 passes) |
| Pipeline barriers | Between upsweep/spine/downsweep | Between histogram/scatter |
| Timestamp count | 2 (single envelope) | 8 (envelope from first to last) |

These are inherent to each algorithm's design and represent real-world performance characteristics.

## Device Info

- **SoC**: Kirin (ARM big.LITTLE, 14 cores)
- **CPU topology**: 4×1.72 GHz (LITTLE) + 8×2.27 GHz (mid) + 2×2.75 GHz (big)
- **GPU**: Maleoon 935, Vulkan 1.4.309
- **subgroupSize**: 32, maxComputeInvocations=1024, maxSharedMemory=32768
- **timestampPeriod**: ~107 ns/tick

## Raw Data

- `vulkan_perf_locked.csv` — vulkan_radix_sort GPU, locked max freq (1K–1M)
- `cpu_perf_locked.csv` — CPU std::sort, locked max freq (1K–1M)

# 两边 Benchmark 的不公平因素分析

## 从代码逐行对比的发现

### ⚠️⚠️⚠️ 不公平因素 1: Buffer 分配/释放 — 每 run 都做

**VkRadixSort**: 每次 execute() 都:
  1. prepareBuffers() — 创建 3 个 GPU buffer (2 个 N×4B ping-pong + 1 个 histogram)
  2. generateRandomNumbers() — CPU 生成随机数
  3. fillDeviceWithStagingBuffer() — staging upload 到 GPU
  4. ... 排序 ...
  5. releaseBuffers() — 销毁 3 个 GPU buffer

  这意味着每个 timed run 都包含:
  - vkCreateBuffer × 3
  - staging allocation × 3
  - vkCmdCopyBuffer upload × 3
  - vkDestroyBuffer × 3

  **在 8M 时**: 分配/释放 3 × 32MB = 96MB GPU 内存 + 96MB staging

**vulkan_radix_sort**: 每次 Sort():
  1. Reallocate() — 只在大小变化时才重新分配
  2. 同一个 staging/keys/storage buffer 跨所有 run 复用
  3. staging upload 仍然每次做

  **在 8M 时**: buffer 复用，只有 staging upload × 1

**影响**: VkRadixSort 每 run 多了 buffer alloc/free 开销。

但 staging upload 的 vkCmdCopyBuffer 是在 GPU timestamp 范围之前完成的...
等等，让我再确认 timestamp 是否包含 upload。

实际上 VkRadixSort 的 timestamp 只包在 execute() 的循环里，
不包含 prepareBuffers()。
所以 alloc/upload 不在 GPU timestamp 内。
但 vrs 的 Sort() 也是 upload → submit → sort → readback，
timestamp 只包 sort 部分。
所以这部分是公平的 — 两者都不包含 upload。

### ⚠️⚠️⚠️ 不公平因素 2: Query Pool 创建/销毁 — 每 run 都做

**VkRadixSort**: 每次 execute() 都:
  - vkCreateQueryPool() — 创建 8 个 query
  - vkResetQueryPool() — 重置
  - ... 排序 ...
  - vkGetQueryPoolResults() — 读取
  - ~QueryPoolGuard() { vkDestroyQueryPool() } — 销毁

**vulkan_radix_sort**: 构造时创建一次:
  - vkCreateQueryPool(query_count=15) — 一次
  - 每次 Sort(): vkCmdResetQueryPool + vkGetQueryPoolResults
  - 析构时销毁一次

**影响**: VkRadixSort 每次多了一次 create + destroy query pool。
但 query pool 开销极小，对 GPU timestamp 无影响。

### ⚠️⚠️⚠️ 不公平因素 3: 命令提交模式 — 4× submit vs 1× submit

**VkRadixSort**: 4 个 iteration，每个:
  - vkWaitForFences (等上一个完成)
  - vkResetFences
  - vkResetCommandBuffer
  - fillCommandBuffer
  - vkQueueSubmit (带 semaphore wait/signal)
  
  总共: 4 次 vkQueueSubmit + 3 次 semaphore chain

**vulkan_radix_sort**: 
  - 1 次 vkQueueSubmit，包含所有 12 个 dispatch 在单个 cmd buffer 里
  
  总共: 1 次 vkQueueSubmit

**影响**: 这是最大的不公平因素！
  - 4 次 submit 的 CPU 开销: 每次 ~几十微秒
  - 3 次 semaphore signal/wait 的 GPU 空闲间隙
  - 每次 submit 之间 GPU 可能有微小空窗期
  - envelope 测量的是 first→last timestamp，
    但中间的 semaphore 等待可能导致 GPU 在 iteration 间空转

### ⚠️⚠️ 不公平因素 4: 双缓冲 activeIndex 切换

**VkRadixSort**: 使用 double-buffering (activeIndex / activeIndex+1),
每个 iteration 都 incrementActiveIndex()。
这导致:
  - 4 个 iteration 交替使用 2 套 command buffer/fence/semaphore
  - 每个 iteration 的 fence wait 可能等错的对象

**vulkan_radix_sort**: 单一 command buffer + fence，每次完全串行。

**影响**: 可能导致 VkRadixSort 的 fence 等待时间更长，
因为 double buffering 在串行模式下反而增加了等待。
但 GPU timestamp 不包含 fence wait。

### ⚠️⚠️ 不公平因素 5: Fence Wait 在 Timestamp 之前

**VkRadixSort ComputePass::executeInternal()**:
  Line 84: vkWaitForFences() — 等上一个完成
  Line 85: vkResetFences()
  Line 87: vkResetCommandBuffer()
  Line 88: fillCommandBuffer() — 这里写 timestamp
  Line 103: vkQueueSubmit()

  问题: vkWaitForFences 在 timestamp 之前！
  对于第 2-4 个 iteration，fence wait 是等上一个 iteration 的 GPU 完成。
  这本身不在 GPU timestamp 内，但它确保了顺序执行。

  **但关键问题**: 每个 iteration 的 vkQueueSubmit 是独立的 submit。
  GPU 在两个 submit 之间可能有空窗期（semaphore 延迟）。
  这个空窗期被 envelope timestamp 捕获了！

### ⚠️ 不公平因素 6: Storage Buffer 总量

**VkRadixSort**: 
  - buffer0: N × 4B (keys ping-pong)
  - buffer1: N × 4B (keys ping-pong) 
  - buffer2: num_WG × 256 × 4B (histograms)
  总计: 2N × 4B + num_WG × 1KB

  8M 时: 64MB + 1MB = 65MB

**vulkan_radix_sort** (从 vrdxGetSorterStorageRequirements):
  - keys: N × 4B (input/output)
  - storage: 包含 internal buffers (global histogram, partition histograms 等)
  总计约: N × 4B + 一些固定大小的 buffer

  8M 时: ~32MB + 几 KB

**影响**: VkRadixSort 使用 2× 的 GPU 内存（ping-pong buffer），
可能对 GPU cache 和 memory controller 造成更大压力。

### ⚠️ 不公平因素 7: Descriptor Set 更新频率

**VkRadixSort**: 每个 iteration 都要更新 descriptor sets
  (setStorageBuffer × 6 次 per execute，但在循环外设置)
  然后每个 iteration 用不同的 activeIndex 绑定不同 descriptor set

**vulkan_radix_sort**: vrdxCmdSort 内部处理所有 descriptor 绑定，
push descriptor (VK_KHR_push_descriptor) 可以避免 descriptor set 分配。

**影响**: 如果 vrs 用了 push descriptor 而 vkr 用传统 descriptor set，
vkr 会有额外开销。

### ✅ 公平因素确认

1. 两者都用 GPU timestamp envelope，不在 CPU overhead 内
2. 两者都 5 warmup + 10 timed median
3. 两者都 full 32-bit random range
4. 两者都用 ALL_COMMANDS_BIT timestamp
5. 两者都 pipeline 创建一次复用
6. 两者都 verification pass（不在 timestamp 内）

## 真正影响 GPU timestamp 测量的不公平因素（从大到小）

1. **4× vkQueueSubmit + semaphore chain** — 最大不公平
   GPU 在 iteration 间的 semaphore 等待会产生空窗期
   envelope 捕获了这些空窗期
   估计影响: 每个空窗期 ~几十微秒 × 3 = ~0.1ms

2. **2× GPU 内存占用** (ping-pong buffer)
   VkRadixSort 的 scatter 在写 buffer1 时需要同时读 buffer0
   对 cache/TLB 压力更大
   在 8M 时 ping-pong = 64MB，接近或超过 GPU cache 容量

3. **Descriptor set 绑定方式** (可能)
   需要确认 vrs 是否用了 push descriptor
"""

print(analysis)

确认了。现在来量化这些不公平因素的影响：

## 不公平因素完整分析

### 🔴 因素 1：4× submit + semaphore chain vs 1× submit（最大不公平）

| | vulkan_radix_sort | VkRadixSort |
|---|---|---|
| vkQueueSubmit | **1 次** | **4 次** |
| Semaphore wait/signal | 无 | **3 次 chain** |
| 命令缓冲区 | 1 个（含 12 dispatch） | 4 个（各含 2 dispatch） |

**GPU timestamp envelope 捕获了 submit 间的空窗期。** 每次 submit→semaphore signal→下一个 submit 的 semaphore wait，GPU 会空转等待。这在 Maleoon 935 单 compute queue 上尤其明显 — 下一个 iteration 必须等上一个完全结束才能开始。

**估计影响**：每次 submit 间隙 ~10-30μs × 3 ≈ **0.03-0.09ms**。在小 N 时占比大（1K 时总共才 0.39ms），大 N 时占比小。

### 🔴 因素 2：GPU 内存占用 — 2× vs 1×

| | vulkan_radix_sort | VkRadixSort |
|---|---|---|
| Keys buffer | N × 4B（原地排序） | 2 × N × 4B（ping-pong） |
| 8M 时 | ~32 MB | **~64 MB** |
| Histogram | 固定大小 | num_WG × 1KB |
| 总计 8M | ~32 MB | **~65 MB** |

VkRadixSort 的 ping-pong 设计需要同时持有 input 和 output buffer（scatter 写入另一个 buffer）。8M 时 64MB 工作集对 GPU cache/TLB 压力远大于 vrs 的 32MB。

### 🟡 因素 3：Push Descriptor vs 传统 Descriptor Set

```
vrs: VK_KHR_push_descriptor — 每次 dispatch 直接 push，无需分配/更新 descriptor set
vkr: 传统 vkCmdBindDescriptorSets — 预分配 descriptor set，绑定
```

Maleoon 935 支持 `VK_KHR_push_descriptor`，vrs 用了，vkr 没用。Push descriptor 避免了 descriptor set 的 allocation/write 开销，但 GPU 执行时间差异很小。

### 🟡 因素 4：Buffer 每 run 分配/释放 vs 复用

虽然不在 GPU timestamp 内（timestamp 只测排序），但 VkRadixSort 每个 timed run 分配 3 个大 buffer + staging upload + 销毁，在 8M 时是 96MB alloc + 96MB free。这些操作可能触发 GPU driver 的内存管理开销（碎片整理、page table 更新等），间接影响后续 GPU 执行的 memory mapping。

### 🟢 因素 5：Query Pool 每 run 创建/销毁

VkRadixSort 每 run 创建/销毁一个 8-query pool，vrs 创建一次复用。开销极小，可忽略。

### 🟢 已确认公平的因素

- ✅ GPU timestamp envelope（ALL_COMMANDS_BIT）
- ✅ 5 warmup + 10 median
- ✅ Full 32-bit random
- ✅ Pipeline 复用
- ✅ Verification 不在 timestamp 内
- ✅ 全频锁定（GPU 933 + DDR 4.8 + CPU 2.75 GHz）

---

### 能否修正这些不公平？

| 因素 | 可修正？ | 方案 |
|------|---------|------|
| 4× submit | ✅ | 把 4 个 iteration 录入同一个 command buffer，消除 semaphore |
| 2× 内存 | ❌ | ping-pong 是 scatter 算法的固有设计，无法避免 |
| Push descriptor | ⚠️ | 需要改 vkr 的 engine 层，侵入性大 |
| Buffer 复用 | ✅ | 改为 buffer 大小只增不减，跨 run 复用 |
| Query pool 复用 | ✅ | 创建一次复用 |

**因素 1（4× submit）是最值得修正的**，因为它是测量层面（而非算法层面）的不公平。如果我们把 VkRadixSort 的 4 个 iteration 合并到一个 command buffer 里提交，就能在相同条件下（1× submit）比较纯算法性能。要改吗？

数据非常清晰：

### Submit 间隙的影响

**submit 间隙是固定的 ~0.034ms × 3 ≈ 0.1ms**（与 N 无关），所以：

| N 范围 | 间隙占 envelope 比例 | 影响 |
|--------|---:|------|
| **1K** | **33.3%** | 非常大！envelope 比实际计算慢 1/3 |
| **2K** | **29.6%** | 将近 1/3 是空转 |
| 4K–16K | 16–21% | 仍然显著 |
| 64K–256K | 1–4% | 较小 |
| 1M–8M | **<0.5%** | 可忽略 |

### 两种计时方式的比较

| N | vkr sum（纯GPU计算） | vkr envelope（含submit间隙） | vrs | **sum/vrs** | **envelope/vrs** |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1K | 0.266 | 0.399 | 0.287 | **0.93×** | 1.39× |
| 2K | 0.301 | 0.428 | 0.295 | **1.02×** | 1.45× |
| 4K | 0.372 | 0.473 | 0.298 | 1.25× | 1.59× |
| 8K | 0.512 | 0.548 | 0.308 | 1.66× | 1.78× |
| 32K | 0.532 | 0.568 | 0.442 | **1.20×** | 1.28× |
| 1M | 9.221 | 9.256 | 7.535 | **1.22×** | 1.23× |
| 8M | 133.426 | 133.460 | 57.050 | **2.34×** | 2.34× |

### 关键发现

1. **用 sum 对比时，小 N 的差距大幅缩小**
   - 1K: envelope 说 vkr 慢 39%，但实际计算只慢 **7%**
   - 2K: envelope 说 vkr 慢 45%，但实际计算 vkr **几乎打平**（1.02×）

2. **大 N（≥1M）两种计时方式结果一致** — submit 间隙占比 <0.5%，可忽略

3. **vkr 在 1K-2K 的纯计算时间确实和 vrs 接近** — 这符合预期：8 dispatch vs 12 dispatch，少了 spine pass 的开销

4. **真正的算法差距从 8K 开始显现**，且随 N 增大而增大（1.66× → 2.34×）

### 结论

**vkr 的 sum 是更公平的对比基准**，因为它和 vrs 的 envelope 一样测的是纯 GPU 计算时间（不含 submit 间隙）。当前文档里用的 envelope 对 vkr 小 N 的结果不公平（虚高了 10-33%）。

content.text:
看到了所有改动。你做了三个修改：

1. **加了 `vkCmdFillBuffer` + `vkCmdUpdateBuffer` + barrier** 在第一次 pass 内 — 匹配 vrs 的 setup overhead
2. **`NUM_BLOCKS_PER_WORKGROUP` 改为可配置，默认 24** — 降低每 WG 元素数以增加并行度
3. **环境变量 `VKR_BLOCKS`** — 可调整

还有以下不公平因素：

### 仍然存在的公平问题

**🔴 问题 1：仍然是 4× submit + semaphore chain（最大的不公平没有改）**

代码里 `for (i = 0..3)` 仍然调用 `m_pass->execute()` 4 次，每次都是独立的 `vkQueueSubmit` + semaphore chain。每个 iteration 之间 GPU 必须等 semaphore signal→wait 才能开始下一个，这个空窗期被 envelope 捕获了。

vrs 是 **1 个 command buffer 包含 12 个 dispatch + 内部 barrier**，只 submit 一次。

**要修**：需要把 4 个 iteration 的 histogram + scatter 全部录入同一个 command buffer，只用一次 `vkQueueSubmit`。这样 GPU 可以在内部 barrier 间无缝切换，消除 semaphore 空窗。

**🟡 问题 2：Buffer 每 run 仍然分配/释放**

`prepareBuffers()` + `releaseBuffers()` 仍在每次 `execute()` 中调用。8M 时每次分配/释放 64MB+。虽然不在 GPU timestamp 内，但频繁 alloc/free 会增加 GPU driver 内存管理压力。

**🟡 问题 3：Query Pool 仍然每 run 创建/销毁**

content.text:
结论非常清晰：

### Single-submit 的效果

| N 范围 | Single-submit 加速 | 说明 |
|---------|:-:|---|
| **1K–4K** | **1.29–1.53×** | 消除 3 次 semaphore 空窗期，效果最大 |
| 8K–32K | 1.05–1.20× | 仍有改善 |
| **≥512K** | **~1.00×** | 无差异 |

在小 N 时，4×submit 的 semaphore 空窗期占总时间比例大（1K 时 ~0.13ms / 0.39ms ≈ 33%），消除后显著改善。大 N 时排序本身占主导，submit 开销可忽略。

### 消除 submit 不公平后的公平对比（BLOCKS=32）

| N | vkr/vrs | 说明 |
|---:|:-:|---|
| 1K | 0.90× | **vkr 首次在小 N 赢了 vrs！** |
| 2K | **1.00×** | 完全打平 |
| 32K | 1.19× | vrs 领先 19% |
| 1M | 1.22× | vrs 领先 22% |
| **8M** | **2.33×** | vrs 领先 133%，纯算法差距 |

消除 submit 不公平后，vkr 在 1K–2K 反超 vrs（更少的 dispatch 次数），大 N 的差距完全来自算法本身。4M→8M 的 3.47× 退化也被确认为纯算法问题。

CPU 和 vrs 没有改过，无需重跑。要更新文档和图表推送吗？

# Radix Sort Benchmark Results — Maleoon 935

Date: 2026-06-11

## Test Environment

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| **Device** | HarmonyOS arm64 phone |
| **GPU** | Maleoon 935, Vulkan 1.4.309, subgroupSize=32 |
| **GPU freq** | Locked 933 MHz (was 235 MHz under DVFS auto) |
| **DDR freq** | Locked 4800 MHz (was 1066 MHz under DVFS auto) |
| **L1 bus freq** | Locked 1172 MHz |
| **CPU** | Kirin big.LITTLE: 4×1.72 GHz + 8×2.27 GHz + 2×2.75 GHz |
| **CPU freq** | All 14 cores locked to max |
| **CPU sort** | `std::sort` / `std::stable_sort`, pinned to big cores (cpu12-13, 2.75 GHz) |
| **GPU timing** | `vkCmdWriteTimestamp` (ALL_COMMANDS_BIT) × `timestampPeriod` (~107 ns/tick), envelope |
| **CPU timing** | `std::chrono::high_resolution_clock` for `std::sort` |
| **Build** | HarmonyOS NDK cross-compiled, `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` |
| **Sizes** | 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K, 32K, 64K, 128K, 256K, 512K, 1M, 2M, 4M, 8M |

## DVFS Locking

All DVFS domains locked to maximum frequency via sysfs:

```
GPU:  echo 933000000  > /sys/class/devfreq/gpufreq/{min,max}_freq        (235 → 933 MHz)
DDR:  echo 4800000000 > /sys/class/devfreq/ddrfreq/{min,max}_freq        (1066 → 4800 MHz)
DDRL: echo 4800000000 > /sys/class/devfreq/ddrfreq_latency/{min,max}_freq
BUS:  echo 1172000000 > /sys/class/devfreq/ddrfreq_l1bus_latency/{min,max}_freq
CPU:  echo $max_freq   > /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_min_freq
```

DVFS auto mode had GPU running at 235 MHz (25% of max) and DDR at 1066 MHz (22% of max) during idle. Locking all domains removes frequency as a variable, making measurements deterministic and reproducible.

## Algorithms Compared

| Algorithm | Source | Dispatch/Pass | Pipeline | Submit | Warmup | Runs |
|-----------|--------|---------------|----------|--------|--------|------|
| **CPU std::sort** | C++ STL | — | — | — | 5 | 10 (median) |
| **vulkan_radix_sort** | [vulkan_radix_sort](.) | 3 dispatch/pass (upsweep→spine→downsweep) × 4 passes | Created once | **1×** | 5 | 10 (median) |
| **VkRadixSort Multi** | [VkRadixSort](../VkRadixSort) | 2 dispatch/pass (histogram→scatter) × 4 passes | Created once (reused) | **1×** (single cmd buffer) | 5 | 10 (median) |

Both GPU radix sorts operate on 32-bit unsigned integers (full range `[0, 2³²-1]`) with 4 × 8-bit radix passes and `WORKGROUP_SIZE=256`.

## Timing Methodology

Both GPU implementations use `vkCmdWriteTimestamp` with `VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_ALL_COMMANDS_BIT` to measure the **envelope** time from first to last timestamp, both recorded in a **single command buffer** submitted once:

- **vulkan_radix_sort**: 2 timestamps around the entire sort (12 dispatch + internal barriers)
- **VkRadixSort Multi**: 2 timestamps around all 4 iterations (8 dispatch + internal barriers)

This eliminates any submit/semaphore overhead from the measurement, capturing only GPU compute + internal barrier time.

## Full Comparison (All Frequencies Locked, Single Submit)

![Three-way comparison](benchmark_comparison_full.png)

### Keys-only Sort (GPU timestamp envelope, median of 10 runs)

| N | CPU (ms) | vulkan_radix_sort (ms) | VkRadixSort Multi (ms) | vrs/CPU | vkr/CPU | vkr/vrs |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1K | 0.039 | 0.286 | 0.257 | 0.14× | 0.15× | **0.90×** |
| 2K | 0.080 | 0.291 | 0.294 | 0.27× | 0.27× | **1.01×** |
| 4K | 0.169 | 0.296 | 0.367 | 0.57× | 0.46× | 1.24× |
| **8K** | **0.357** | **0.304** | **0.509** | **1.17×** | 0.70× | 1.67× |
| **16K** | **0.773** | **0.313** | **0.516** | **2.47×** | **1.50×** | 1.65× |
| **32K** | **1.666** | **0.440** | **0.524** | **3.79×** | **3.18×** | 1.19× |
| 64K | 3.549 | 0.627 | 0.823 | 5.66× | 4.31× | 1.31× |
| 128K | 7.505 | 1.111 | 1.271 | 6.76× | 5.90× | 1.14× |
| 256K | 15.963 | 2.140 | 2.367 | 7.46× | 6.74× | 1.11× |
| 512K | 34.155 | 3.924 | 4.590 | 8.70× | 7.44× | 1.17× |
| **1M** | **71.957** | **7.530** | **9.216** | **9.56×** | **7.81×** | 1.22× |
| **2M** | **151.249** | **14.660** | **19.007** | **10.32×** | **7.96×** | 1.30× |
| **4M** | **314.482** | **28.831** | **38.370** | **10.91×** | **8.20×** | 1.33× |
| **8M** | **689.529** | **57.240** | **133.113** | **12.05×** | **5.18×** | **2.33×** |

> **vrs/CPU** = CPU time / vulkan_radix_sort time (>1 = GPU faster)
> **vkr/CPU** = CPU time / VkRadixSort time (>1 = GPU faster)
> **vkr/vrs** = VkRadixSort time / vulkan_radix_sort time (>1 = vulkan_radix_sort faster, <1 = VkRadixSort faster)

### Key-Value Sort (vulkan_radix_sort only)

| N | CPU kv (ms) | vrs kv GPU (ms) | GPU Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1K | 0.055 | 0.314 | 0.18× |
| 2K | 0.120 | 0.327 | 0.37× |
| 4K | 0.219 | 0.329 | 0.67× |
| **8K** | **0.514** | **0.340** | **1.51×** |
| **16K** | **1.036** | **0.357** | **2.90×** |
| **32K** | **2.382** | **0.527** | **4.52×** |
| 64K | 4.812 | 0.780 | 6.17× |
| 128K | 11.114 | 1.459 | 7.62× |
| 256K | 22.171 | 3.060 | 7.25× |
| 512K | 50.724 | 5.672 | 8.94× |
| **1M** | **106.556** | **11.030** | **9.66×** |
| **2M** | **251.300** | **21.694** | **11.58×** |
| **4M** | **529.222** | **43.150** | **12.27×** |
| **8M** | **1258.716** | **85.551** | **14.71×** |

### Scaling Curves

![Scaling comparison](benchmark_comparison_scaling.png)

## Key Findings

### 1. VkRadixSort Wins at Small N

With single command buffer submission (eliminating the submit/semaphore unfairness), VkRadixSort actually wins at the smallest sizes:

| N | vkr/vrs | Winner |
|---:|:-:|---|
| **1K** | **0.90×** | **VkRadixSort wins by 10%** |
| **2K** | **1.01×** | **Essentially tied** |
| 4K | 1.24× | vulkan_radix_sort |

VkRadixSort's advantage at small N comes from fewer dispatches per pass (2 vs 3), meaning lower fixed overhead per radix iteration. The GPU latency floor is 0.257ms (vkr) vs 0.286ms (vrs).

### 2. Crossover Points

| Algorithm | Crossover N | Speedup at Crossover |
|-----------|:-----------:|:--------------------:|
| vulkan_radix_sort | **8K** | 1.17× |
| VkRadixSort Multi | **16K** | 1.50× |

### 3. Peak Performance (N=8M, All Locked)

| Sort | GPU (ms) | CPU (ms) | GPU Speedup | Throughput |
|------|--------:|--------:|------------:|-----------:|
| **vulkan_radix_sort keys** | 57.24 | 689.53 | **12.05×** | **147 MItems/s** |
| **vulkan_radix_sort kv** | 85.55 | 1258.72 | **14.71×** | 98 MItems/s |
| VkRadixSort Multi keys | 133.11 | 689.53 | 5.18× | 63 MItems/s |
| CPU std::sort | — | 689.53 | 1.00× | 12 MItems/s |

### 4. Scaling Analysis

How time grows when data doubles (ideal = 2.00×):

| Transition | CPU | vulkan_radix_sort | VkRadixSort |
|:----------:|:---:|:-----------------:|:-----------:|
| 1M → 2M | 2.10× | **1.95×** | 2.06× |
| 2M → 4M | 2.08× | **1.97×** | 2.02× |
| 4M → 8M | 2.19× | **1.99×** | **3.47×** ⚠️ |

**vulkan_radix_sort scales nearly linearly** (1.95–1.99×) — the GPU is not yet saturated even at 8M, maintaining 139–147 MItems/s throughput.

**VkRadixSort degrades at 4M→8M**: time grows 3.47× for 2× data. Root cause: the scatter shader reads ALL workgroup histograms from global memory for prefix sum — at 8M with 1024 workgroups, this is 1024 × 256 × 4 bytes = 1 MB of global memory reads per workgroup, totaling ~1 GB across all workgroups.

### 5. Why the Gap Widens at Large N

| Factor | vulkan_radix_sort | VkRadixSort Multi |
|--------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Global prefix sum | Dedicated spine pass (fixed 32 WG) | Scatter inlines O(num_WG) global reads |
| WG-internal ranking | **subgroup ballot** (hardware, zero cost) | bin_flags 8 KB shared memory |
| Atomics per element | ~1/32 (waveOffset==0 only) | 1 atomicAdd per element |
| Memory per sort | N × 4B (in-place) | 2N × 4B (ping-pong) |
| Workgroup granularity | 2048 elem/WG | 8192 elem/WG |

### 6. CPU Scaling

CPU `std::sort` at locked 2.75 GHz follows O(N log N) exactly. The normalized time T/(N·log₂N) converges to **~3.4 ns** for N ≥ 16K, which is ~9.4 clock cycles per comparison-swap on the Cortex core.

## Fair Comparison Methodology

All measurements use identical methodology:

1. **Same warmup**: 5 warmup runs before timing (both implementations)
2. **Same repeat count**: Median of 10 timed runs (both implementations)
3. **Same data range**: Full 32-bit `[0, 2³²-1]` uniform random integers (both implementations)
4. **Same timestamp stage**: `VK_PIPELINE_STAGE_ALL_COMMANDS_BIT` for all timestamps
5. **Same measurement type**: GPU timestamp envelope (first→last timestamp), not per-pass sum
6. **Same pipeline policy**: Vulkan pipeline created once, reused across all sizes
7. **Same submit pattern**: Both use **single command buffer, single submit** (no semaphores)
8. **Same frequency**: All DVFS domains locked to max (GPU 933 MHz, DDR 4.8 GHz, CPU 2.75 GHz)
9. **Correctness verified**: Each run verified against CPU `std::sort` result
